draft.title: Present value of an annuity
card: The present value of an annuity is the lump sum needed now to fund a series of equal future payments, when the money earns compound interest.
Each payment is discounted back to today. A payment N made n periods from now is worth N ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ today, where r is the rate per period.
Add the discounted payments to get the present value. Example: $1000 at the end of each year for 3 years at 5% p.a. gives 1000/1.05 + 1000/1.05² + 1000/1.05³ = 952.38 + 907.03 + 863.84 = $2723.25.
Later payments are discounted by more periods, so each is worth less today than the one before.
draft.remember: Present value is the sum of each payment divided by (1 + r)ⁿ for its own n.

a.q: Amir will be paid $2000 in 2 years. Interest is 10% p.a. compounded annually. What is that payment worth today?
a.why: Discount over 2 periods: 2000 ÷ 1.1² = 2000 ÷ 1.21 = $1652.89. Dividing by 1.1 only once ($1818.18) discounts for just one year, but the payment is two years away.
a.clue: Divide by (1 + r) once for each period until payment.

b.q: Lena wants to receive $500 at the end of each year for 2 years. Money earns 8% p.a. compounded annually. What lump sum is needed now?
b.why: Discount each payment separately: 500 ÷ 1.08 = 462.96 and 500 ÷ 1.08² = 428.67, which total $891.63. Discounting the $1000 total by 2 years ($857.34) treats the first payment as if it came a year later than it does.
b.clue: The first payment is discounted by 1 year, the second by 2.

check.summary: No problems found. The card example, both answers and both explanations check out arithmetically.
